notes: A running account of where things stand by these headlines, revised after each edition rather than added to. Every version is kept.
Written by the model from the narratives, not from the headlines. It is a reading, not a record.
standing: By headlines of 20 November, a day after Trump, Xi and Putin issued their Shenzhen declaration, Estonia set 1 December to close its border crossings with Russia, Sweden scrambled jets over Poland after Russian projectiles fell there, and Japan's foreign minister said the declaration differs from Japan's view. The Nasdaq closed 5.37% lower, CoreWeave fell below its listing price and Google was reported to have cut a million TPU chips from its 2027 orders. In the same reports Trump threatened US firms building data centres abroad, Christine Lagarde proposed that EU funds take first losses on chip plants and data centres, and CNBC reported Anthropic raising $93.5 billion. German pupils struck against conscription, Gen Z protests returned to hundreds of European cities and France's parliament adopted a law presuming police use of weapons lawful. From the day before, Haiti's forces and Salvadoran troops were fighting gangs, Colombia's president was weighing asking Congress for US troops and Nigeria's lecturers were demanding withheld salaries.
moved: The thread on Europe's security turned on 20 November: a day after allies were read as seeking their own talks with Moscow, its edition reported Estonia closing its Russian crossings from 1 December, Swedish jets over Poland, eleven European armies drilling in Poland and a new Self-Defence Force base approved in Kagoshima. The Chronicle has withdrawn the talks reading as the thread's direction.

A new thread began on states offering to site and underwrite data centres as private money sells: Trump's threat to US firms building abroad, Lagarde's first-loss proposal, Google's reported chip order cut and a 5.37% Nasdaq fall, though CNBC reported Anthropic raising $93.5 billion the same day.

The thread on young protesters returned after seventeen editions, with German pupils striking against conscription and court cases and arrests in France, Greece and Indonesia. A 31 October expectation of a shared protest date across Europe was kept when DW reported Gen Z protests in hundreds of European cities on 20 November.

A 5 November expectation of the soldiers thread was kept when La Dépêche reported France's parliament definitively adopting the law presuming police use of weapons lawful; the headline came in the youth protest narrative, not in the soldiers thread.
silent: The Nvidia export thread has had no narrative since 17 November. On 20 November Financial News named US chip restrictions on China among the causes of the sell-off, in the data centre narrative, and Huang's House hearing is due on 1 December, so this looks like the editions' division more than the world moving on.

The thread on long-range strikes during talks has had no narrative since 17 November. Russian projectiles falling in Poland came on 20 November in the thread on Europe's security; whether strikes on crossings have stopped these headlines do not say.

Europe's living-cost protests have had no narrative since 17 November, but on 20 November Gen Z marches across Europe and Bologna's general strike day came in the thread on young protesters, so the ground is still reported.
The Iran war thread stays silent since 11 November. No narrative on 19 or 20 November carried the Gulf; whether that is quiet in the war or in the sample these headlines do not say.

threads.label: Iran war, oil prices, talks and reach
threads.text: On 26 October the join was the Gulf running talks and strike preparations. From 27 October to 5 November it followed the Hormuz price shock to jet fuel, mortgages, wages and rates, though no midterm report by 10 November named fuel prices. The war was reported paused on 8 November; on 10 November oil fell on talk of talks; on 11 November producers invested as if Hormuz would stay unsafe. Since then its events have come in other threads: a claimed strike on a US radar in Bahrain on 13 November, a Dutch fertiliser shortage on 14 November, a US strike on Qeshm on 17 November, and on 18 November Iranian strikes on US assets in Kuwait, Bahrain and a UAE tanker. On 19 November the Shenzhen declaration was reported to leave out the Middle East. It is silent by the editions' division.
threads.direction: After a pause reported on 8 November and a turn to talks and a falling price, by 17 and 18 November the US and Iran were reported striking each other again, at Qeshm, Bahrain, Kuwait and a UAE tanker, while talks were said to continue.

threads.label: Governments setting pump prices mid-war
threads.text: Begun on 7 November: Italy would not extend its diesel excise cut, Portugal adjusted its fuel tax discount and Taiwan's CPC held pump prices after absorbing NT$34.07 billion, joined as governments handing the war's fuel price back to drivers. After four editions without a narrative the Chronicle revived it on 12 November with an unlinked narrative marked firm: Pakistan cut petrol and diesel prices, Chile resubmitted a bill freezing fuel prices until February, Greece set €32 million for islanders' sea transport and Indonesian ferry operators asked to raise fares, with crude below $90. Its case against says the decisions move in different directions and none names Hormuz. No narrative has carried it since 12 November, so it is silent; its expectations run to early December.
threads.direction: It has moved from governments ending fuel tax cuts to governments keeping pump prices in their own hands and paying the gap from budgets as crude fell below $90.

threads.label: War energy shock turned into equipment orders
threads.text: Begun on 6 November and not linked by its edition to the Iran thread, though it starts from the same war. Iran says two tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Siemens Energy says a Middle East power push is straining gas turbine supply, a Chinese solar cell line runs at full capacity, Adani Green turns to batteries for India's grid, and an agency finds the energy crisis speeding renewables in emerging economies. The join is that buyers who cannot lower the price of imported fuel are buying equipment to need less of it. Its case against says Siemens Energy's backlog and China's solar capacity predate the war. No narrative has carried it since 6 November, so it is silent. Gas sought beside electrification began a separate thread on 10 November.

threads.label: Housing: state drives, outside money and work
threads.text: On 27 October one narrative joined Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu expanding housing with Portugal investigating police at housing protests. On 6 November the Chronicle revived it, by judgment, when foreign buyers made 16% of Portuguese purchases as prices hit records. On 11 November it was revived again, by judgment, with a narrative marked tentative: millions of Spaniards struck over housing three weeks before a general election, a rush of withdrawals hit China's payroll housing fund, and employer-linked homes were offered in Tianhe and Taiwan. Its case against says Spain has a shortage and China a slump. On 17 November Spain's strike and Porto's housing camp came in a new thread on Europe's weekly protests, which joins them with wages and prices; the Chronicle has not revived this thread for it.
threads.direction: It has moved from states building homes, to prices set by buyers from outside, to housing argued over through strikes, payroll funds and employers.

threads.label: Shared systems failing, from outages to patches
threads.text: Begun on 29 October with Samsung and CHPT profits on data centre demand, it ran through AI-led US growth, borrowing and the Nvidia case to 12 November. From 12 November it followed shared systems stopping: a Microsoft outage at British councils and Australia's federal police, the FAA's nationwide halt, the fallback left to households on 14 November, and on 17 November faults hard to tell from attacks. On 18 November it named a cause: South Korea's Digital Daily blamed a flood of patches for AI-found flaws for failures at the NSA, in finance and in aviation, and the FBI warned that an AI tool can finish an attack in three hours. No narrative carried it on 19 or 20 November; on 20 November data centres returned in a thread of their own, as public money. Its case against says the patch cause rests on one outlet.
threads.direction: It has moved from profit and borrowing to public services stopping when one system fails, to who holds the backup, to telling a fault from an attack, and by 18 November to patches for AI-found flaws named as a cause.

threads.label: AI labs financed by suppliers, then public shareholders
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 10 November: TSMC was reported investing NT$32 billion in OpenAI and Anthropic as Anthropic's draft prospectus showed a listing of up to $64.4 billion. Its expectation that Anthropic would cut or delay its listing failed on 17 November. The Chronicle revived it on 18 November for an unlinked narrative: Anthropic priced at $83 a share, a $1.5 trillion valuation, as the ECB compared the AI build to subprime. On 19 November Anthropic passed $3 trillion on its first day, Wall Street closed sharply lower and Taiwan's index fell below 40,000 with 45 settlement defaults. On 20 November, in the new data centre thread and not here, the Nasdaq fell 5.37%, CoreWeave dropped below its listing price and CNBC reported Anthropic raising $93.5 billion. Its case against says large first-day rises are normal for new listings.
threads.direction: It has moved from chip suppliers funding the AI labs, to the labs selling shares to the public at record prices, to who took the first-day gain while other technology shares fell.

threads.label: Courts and heads of state given the last word
threads.text: Begun on 1 November and marked tentative: Poland's president and Tusk's government fighting over the Constitutional Tribunal, Egypt's debate on amending the constitution and Madeira's revision; its case against said only Poland's was a crisis. After six editions without a narrative the Chronicle revived it on 7 November, by judgment: lawyers say Vučić's pardons could go to Serbian courts and Strasbourg, Malaysia's Attorney General seeks an audience with the King over Najib Razak's pardon, Taiwan's cabinet refuses to countersign an Elderly Welfare Act, and a Nigerian court voids Atiku's candidature. No narrative has carried it since 7 November. On 19 November its 1 November expectation was kept when Financial News reported South Korea's ruling party would push to impeach Supreme Court Chief Justice Jo Hee-de, a move against one member of the court rather than its powers.
threads.direction: It moved from fights over who controls courts and constitutions to who has the last word on pardons and laws already passed.

threads.label: Chinese makers' gains and others' answers
threads.text: Begun on 3 November: SCG's chief executive called China's cheap exports a fact of life, Thailand raised taxes on imported electric cars, and Tata Motors and Iveco formed a group. It was revived on 7 November, by judgment, when Musk said Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck and BYD's Yangwang opened pre-orders for a 2.08 million yuan car. On 8 November its own edition carried it on, with Tesla suspending orders for the Cybertruck's entry version, NIO claiming a car a minute and Yangwang launching in Abu Dhabi. On 10 November, with no narrative, The Independent reported Musk axing the Cybertruck with refunds, keeping the 7 November expectation of another US carmaker cutting an electric pickup, though by Tesla itself. No narrative has carried it since 8 November, and no headline here reports a sale lost to a Chinese maker.
threads.direction: It moved from producers elsewhere merging or taxing to meet Chinese goods, to producers elsewhere retreating, and by 8 November to Chinese makers selling abroad at both the cheap and the luxury end.

threads.label: Parliaments refusing governments' budgets
threads.text: Begun on 5 November. French deputies unanimously rejected their government's budget ahead of nationwide wage strikes, and Senegal's parliament asked for the 2027 budget bill to be withdrawn. Rob Jetten warned Dutch MPs that voting down his tax plan would cost billions, Japan's prime minister faces a time-limited committee session over a consumption tax cut, and a Democratic Congress must now fund the US government. The join is that governments no longer command the chambers that pass next year's taxes and spending. Its case against says autumn is budget season, first-reading rejections are common, and only the French and Senegalese cases are outright refusals. No narrative has carried it since 5 November, so it is silent; the Japanese cut bears on an expectation open to 28 November.

threads.label: Soldiers sent against disorder, gangs and smugglers
threads.text: Begun on 5 November, marked tentative: Indonesia's troops in Jakarta, the army's account of a riot in Aceh, Pakistan's army for Punjab by-elections, a Bangladeshi soldier killed raiding traffickers at Teknaf, Lebanese army raids and a French bill widening when police may fire. After eleven editions without a narrative it was resumed on 19 November, marked plausible, as crime fought as war: Haiti's forces fought gangs for a corridor with Salvadoran troops in the country, Colombia's president counted a tenth bombing and weighed asking Congress for US troops, fishermen sued Washington over a drone strike at sea and the OAS called a session on organised crime. On 20 November La Dépêche reported France's parliament definitively adopting the law presuming police use of weapons lawful, keeping the 5 November expectation; the headline came in the youth protest thread. Its case against says the military role in each is decades old.
threads.direction: It has moved from soldiers keeping order on home streets to armies, aircraft and foreign troops fighting gangs and smugglers, with results counted as deaths and strikes.

threads.label: Regulators targeting platforms' recommendation systems
threads.text: Begun on 6 November. The European Commission accused TikTok of breaching EU rules through its content recommendation system, and Google, Meta and TikTok are suing to block a California law restricting addictive social media features for children. China's broadcasting regulator opened a two-month campaign against vulgar and homogenised AI micro-dramas after removing 75,000 titles, and Democrats are preparing AI bills for Congress. The join is that the thing regulated is the system choosing what a user sees next, not a single post. Its case against says the three regulators want different things and only the EU and California cases are clearly about ranking design. No narrative has carried it since 6 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Failed banks and money cases reaching office
threads.text: Begun on 6 November. Paraguay's Congress resumed impeachment of President Santiago Peña over the Ueno bank crisis, Daniel Vorcaro's phone recorded 316 interactions with Justice Alexandre de Moraes in the Banco Master case, and UMNO's move to pay Najib Razak's RM50 million fine split Malaysia's coalition. On 8 November an unlinked narrative, placed here by the Chronicle, reported a court freezing the assets of Peña, described as former president, and his arrest over an estimated $809 million Ueno loss, with the Philippine vice-president answering wealth charges and opponents in Armenia and Egypt facing courts. No narrative has carried it since 8 November. On 12 November Sara Duterte's impeachment trial appeared in the new thread on leaders' children.
threads.direction: It moved from failed banks reaching people in office to courts reaching office-holders through money in general, with Peña going from impeachment proceedings to arrest in two days.

threads.label: El Niño's first weeks arriving as rain
threads.text: Begun on 7 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Keiko Fujimori is reported visiting parts of Peru's Tumbes hit by rain, and Pulzo reports that El Niño has not stopped thunderstorms and hail in Bogotá. La Patria reports a landslide bringing trees down onto an avenue in Manizales, Brazil's Civil Defence has a 72-hour alert out, and a downpour stopped Formula One qualifying at Interlagos. The join is that an El Niño expected as drought is arriving first as rain. Its case against says October and November are wet seasons in Colombia and south-eastern Brazil in any year, only one headline names El Niño, and only the Tumbes rain is out of season. No narrative has carried it since 7 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Routes to work abroad rationed and deadly
threads.text: Begun on 8 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Off Lompoul in northern Senegal a pirogue capsized and at least 21 people died. In Bangladesh a lottery shortlisted 300 applicants for 112 fee-free jobs in Malaysia. A testimony in Portugal's SAPO describes shared rooms and low pay ending a migrant's stay, and in West Bengal Suvendu Adhikari promised to deport every 'Bangladeshi infiltrator'. The join is that a person's attempt to work abroad is rationed by a draw, the sea, wages or expulsion. Its case against says the lottery may be meant to cut out recruitment agents, the shipwreck's destination is not given, and four of seven headlines come from bdnews24. No narrative has carried it since 8 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Gas supply sought beside climate summit targets
threads.text: Begun on 10 November and marked tentative by its own edition. The World Meteorological Organization confirmed the last four years as the hottest on record, and COP31 set out an electrification push as the 1.5C goal slips. Deutsche Welle examined Germany's untapped gas, Japan's and Vietnam's leaders discussed an early start to an LNG project, Argentina awaited $38 billion of investment decisions for Vaca Muerta, and Brazil extended its household cooking gas programme to 2031. The join is governments securing gas while planning to electrify. Its case against says Vaca Muerta and the LNG talks are long-running. No narrative has carried it since 10 November, so it is silent; COP31 in Antalya appeared on 11 November only in the seats thread, over Israel's exclusion.

threads.label: Ukraine talks and who pays in Europe
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 10 November and marked firm by its edition. US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi produced a planned prisoner exchange of 1,000 or 1,500 a side and a US offer of 'NATO-style' security guarantees with $400 million in weapons, while Merz threatened to block the next EU budget unless every member supports Ukraine and Fico called that blackmail. Its case against says Merz's demand may belong to the 2028 to 2034 budget talks. On 11 and 12 November the talks came in the seats thread, on 13 and 17 November in the strikes thread, and on 14 and 19 November in the thread on Europe's security. No narrative has carried the question of who pays since 10 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Pope Leo in politics, restraint on reform
threads.text: Begun on 11 November. Pope Leo XIV left Argentina after a Mass for three million, with Die Welt reporting that Javier Milei is on his own after the Pope's criticism, and arrived in Peru, where the government declared non-working days and Keiko Fujimori invited guests to meet him. In the same days the Vatican halted the reform process in the German diocese of Speyer. The join is one office speaking against a government's policy in South America while limiting lay-led reform in Germany. Its case against says popes have criticised Argentine economic policy for a decade, a diocese without a bishop cannot normally change its own structures, and host governments always declare holidays for papal visits. No narrative has carried it since 11 November, so it is silent; the Peru expectation runs to 20 November.

threads.label: Seats, borders and talks used as pressure
threads.text: Begun on 11 November and marked tentative: the CSTO stripped Armenia of its vote, Turkey excluded Israel from COP31 in Antalya, and Washington and Moscow asked Europe to choose one negotiator for the Ukraine talks. On 12 November it was carried on as entry of every kind: Israel will bar Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Washington's envoys said Europeans would join the next round, and Putin spoke of US visas for Russian Olympians. On 13 November the single-negotiator expectation failed when the EU agreed a team of five countries and EU institutions, which weakens the reading of entry as a bargaining move. Its ground passed on 14 November to the thread on Europe's security bargained elsewhere, which on 19 and 20 November followed allies seeking talks and then fortifying. No narrative has carried it since 12 November, so it is silent.
threads.direction: It moved from seats in alliances and summits to entry of every kind, and on 13 November Europe was admitted to the Ukraine talks on its own terms, against the thread's reading.

threads.label: Leaders' children judged on their own conduct
threads.text: Begun on 12 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned as Indonesia's vice-president over a certificate scandal, Sara Duterte's impeachment trial is to resume after the ASEAN summit, Donald Trump Jr left an adviser's role at Kalshi over a conflict with a rival investment, and Nigeria's president congratulated his son Seyi on a traditional title. The join is what a leader's name entitles a child to hold. Its case against says the cases share a family tie and little else. No narrative has carried it since 12 November, but on 18 November its expectation was kept when R7 reported Brazil's prosecutor-general filing a criminal complaint against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro for slandering Lula in a post about Maduro. A slander complaint fits the expectation more loosely than a resignation would.

threads.label: Nvidia scandal as a chip export enforcement dispute
threads.text: Begun on 13 November with a narrative marked firm that continues nothing, though the Nvidia case ran in the AI spending thread from 10 to 12 November: Bessent blamed Lutnick for Megaspeed not being blacklisted, and the Senate summoned Huang and Lutnick. Resumed on 17 November, marked plausible: Nvidia reported revenue up 103% and a $150bn buyback, its board refused Huang's return, and Huang will testify to the House on 1 December. Washington proposed extending chip controls to Southeast Asia and Megaspeed is under US inquiry, keeping a 10 November expectation of a chip rule naming the Nvidia affair. No narrative has carried it since 17 November, so it is silent; on 20 November Financial News named US chip restrictions on China among the causes of the sell-off, in the data centre thread. Its case against says diversion through Singapore and Malaysia was known before.
threads.direction: It has moved from a dispute between two US departments over who let chips reach China to new duties on the states and firms the chips pass through, while Nvidia's sales grew.

threads.label: Long-range strikes during Russia and Iran talks
threads.text: Begun on 13 November, marked plausible: as the EU named its team for the Ukraine talks, a Ukrainian drone hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, bombs went off in Moscow and Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed a strike on a US radar in Bahrain. Resumed on 17 November, marked tentative, with crossings as targets: the Crimean Bridge twice, Kyiv's bridges with 700,000 households left without power, a rail line to Hungary and Iran's Qeshm Island. On 18 November Iranian strikes on US assets came in the interceptors thread. On 19 November Lenta reported Trump saying Putin is angry at Zelensky over the Crimean Bridge attack, keeping the 17 November expectation. No narrative has carried it since 17 November, so it is silent; on 20 November Russian projectiles falling in Poland came in the thread on Europe's security.
threads.direction: It has moved from strikes on bases, ships and oil sites far from the fronts to strikes on bridges and islands in the days before the three-power meeting, one of which came up after it.

threads.label: Frontier states and allies after the three-power declaration
threads.text: Begun on 14 November, marked plausible: Zelensky said Washington floated Ukraine giving up Donbas for NATO membership, the Kremlin announced the Putin, Xi and Trump meeting, and Russian officials demanded Britain give up its nuclear cover for Europe. Resumed on 19 November: the Shenzhen 'declaration toward peace' by Observador's account left out both wars, Europeans met in Berlin, Putin invited them to Moscow and Japan's prime minister made the first leaders' contact with Russia in seven years. On 20 November its edition carried it on, marked tentative, the other way: Estonia set 1 December to close its Russian crossings, Sweden scrambled jets over Poland after Trump called Russian projectiles there a mistake, eleven European armies drilled in Poland, Kagoshima approved landfill for a Self-Defence Force base and Japan's foreign minister said the declaration differs from Japan's view. Its case against says most of these steps were under way before the meeting.
threads.direction: It has moved from Europe's security bargained in a format Europe does not lead, through allies seeking their own talks with Moscow on 19 November, to frontier states closing borders and building bases on 20 November.

threads.label: Incomes set by rule falling behind prices
threads.text: Begun on 14 November with a narrative marked plausible that continues nothing. France had a fifth Saturday of protests against the cost of living and French police demanded a higher risk allowance; an Italian simulation put a 2028 pension more than 13,000 euros a year below one of twenty years earlier; a former Argentine judge warned of delays in retirees' claims, and a Canadian disability charity closed. The join is incomes fixed by law, decree or grant falling behind prices; its case against says the events share no cause. On 17 November a new thread on Europe's weekly protests took in the same French protest rounds and read them as met by top-ups; the Chronicle kept the two apart. No narrative has carried it since 14 November, so it is silent; on 19 November strikes outside Europe over pay owed began a thread of their own.

threads.label: Governments taking back roles in food supply
threads.text: Begun on 14 November with a narrative marked tentative that continues nothing. Nieuws.nl reports a fertiliser shortage caused by the Hormuz blockade threatening Dutch food security, Marib's farmers in Yemen have harvests and no open markets, Senegal calls rice a pillar of food sovereignty, New York is spending $70 million on five city-run grocery stores, Egypt's prime minister inspects a permanent state food fair, and Fortune reports nearby shops losing sales when Walmart leaves a town. The join is public authorities taking back choosing what is grown, securing inputs and selling food. Its case against says only the fertiliser story is new, Egypt's outlets date from the 1940s and New York's stores were a 2025 election promise. No narrative carried it on 17, 18 or 19 November, so it is silent; its expectations run to 5 and 12 December.

threads.label: Europe's protests over prices, met by top-ups
threads.text: Begun on 17 November with a narrative marked plausible, built from a subject the site's notebook had kept for some days before any narrative, so the story is older than its first narrative. It counts two weeks of protest over living costs and housing: 270,000 marched outside Paris on 6 November, Porto's housing camp put up tents on 8 November, Spain held its first general strike in 14 years on 11 November, and France counted 146,000 at a new round on 17 November. France brought forward a minimum wage rise and Italy's coalition argued over 300 euros for pensioners. Its case against says Spanish rents and French wages have different causes. No narrative has carried it since 17 November, so it is silent; on 20 November Gen Z marches across Europe and Bologna's general strike day came in the thread on young protesters.

threads.label: Defence decided by numbers of drones and interceptors
threads.text: Begun on 30 October with a narrative the Chronicle had not given a thread: cheap drones had made defence a matter of quantity again, so states were financing arms factories and widening conscription. After seventeen editions without a narrative it was resumed on 18 November, marked plausible, from the defending side: an Egyptian military expert told Al-Watan that closing the gap in US Patriot production will take years, the Jerusalem Post reported a rayon shortage threatening that production, Iran struck US assets in Kuwait, Bahrain and a UAE tanker, and a coalition struck the Houthis. Its case against says the Patriot shortfall has been discussed since 2023. No narrative carried it on 19 or 20 November; on 20 November Swedish jets over Poland and German pupils striking against conscription came in other threads.
threads.direction: It has moved from cheap drones driving arms production and conscription to interceptor stocks that factories cannot refill quickly.

threads.label: Others' trade deals while three powers meet
threads.text: Begun on 18 November with a narrative marked plausible that continues nothing, as Trump, Xi and Putin were reported meeting in China. EU governments approved signing their trade agreement with Indonesia, Mark Carney bet on Asia-Pacific trade to reduce Canada's dependencies, Vietnam's leader called for a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, Xi asked Chile to deepen ties, Keiko Fujimori pitched Peru's Chancay port to Chinese investors and Egypt signed an industrial deal with India. The join is governments outside the meeting fixing their trade without waiting on it. Its case against says APEC leaders talk trade every November. On 19 November the meeting ended with a declaration that, by Observador's account, left out both wars, which weakens the picture of three powers bargaining over them. No narrative carried trade on 19 or 20 November.

threads.label: Strikes outside Europe over pay already owed
threads.text: Begun on 19 November with a narrative marked tentative, built from a subject the site's notebook had kept for some days before any narrative, so the story is older than its first narrative. It counts strikes and protests outside Europe since 5 November in Nigeria, Egypt, Bangladesh, Canada, Chile, Mexico and South Korea: on 19 November Nigeria's lecturers demanded withheld salaries, Zamalek's players complained of late dues, Bangladeshi garment workers clashed with police and Niagara's paramedics neared a strike, while the World Bank said Bangladesh is short of revenue. The join is pay already earned or promised and not paid, often by a state short of money. Its case against says several headlines name no cause and the sample leans on three Nigerian papers. No narrative carried it on 20 November.

threads.label: States offering to site and underwrite data centres
threads.text: Begun on 20 November with a narrative marked plausible, built from a subject the site's notebook had kept for some days, so the story is older than its first narrative. Trump threatened to tax or sanction US firms that build data centres abroad, Lagarde said EU funds should take first losses on chip plants and data centres, Google was reported to have cut a million TPU chips from its 2027 orders, CoreWeave fell below its listing price and the Nasdaq closed 5.37% lower. Over the fortnight Brussels warned that Portugal's investment was concentrating in data centres and Texas counted $18 billion of data tax at stake. The join is governments offering to locate and carry the build as private investors sell. It continues nothing, though it takes up ground the systems thread held from 29 October to 5 November. Its case against says CNBC reported Anthropic raising $93.5 billion the same day.

threads.label: Young protesters met by police and courts
threads.text: Begun on 31 October with protests called for the same weekend in several European countries, met with bans in some cities and talks in others; on 1 November its edition read them as Europe's governments meeting young protesters mainly with police numbers. The previous Chronicle did not carry it. After seventeen editions without a narrative it was resumed on 20 November, marked plausible and built from the site's notebook: pupils in Schleswig-Holstein struck against conscription, DW reported Gen Z protests in hundreds of European cities, keeping a 31 October expectation of a shared protest date, a Lormont pupil went before the courts and France adopted its police weapons law, after a fortnight of arrests in Yogyakarta and Athens. Its case against says the protests share an age group, not a cause, and Germany's strikes passed without bans, so the 1 November expectation of a German ban is unmet.
threads.direction: It has moved from police numbers set against young protesters to courts, arrests and suspensions, and in Germany to a plan for military service.

withdrawn.held: AI companies' share listings, the copyright suit against Anthropic and county refusals of data centre land, grid and water formed one thread.
withdrawn.undone: On 29 October data centres returned on their own, as profit for Samsung and CHPT and as planning and security disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia, with no listing or lawsuit in view. The land and power question is running apart from the companies' finance and courts, so the merge no longer holds.

withdrawn.held: The Iran war's price rise was moving outward from the pump to central bank rates and loan contracts, with the war named less often at each step.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the reports ran the other way: Washington pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries and sending Tehran a peace proposal, Israel's pump price set to fall, Russia budgeting on $50 oil and US mortgage rates down for two weeks. The war was named directly again, and the costs were reported as easing more than spreading.

withdrawn.held: The data centre question was running apart from the AI companies' finance, as a matter of land, power and security.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the data centre thread itself turned to finance: US growth credited to AI investment, Amazon's spending and Alphabet's fall in market value, with no planning or security dispute in that edition. The split of threads stands, but the separation of data centres from company finance does not.

withdrawn.held: On 30 October the Iran war's costs had turned towards easing, with Washington pressing for a lower oil price before the midterms.
withdrawn.undone: On 31 October Brent rose 2.4% to $117.64, Italy's inflation reached 5.4% and the price rise was argued over in pay rounds and tax relief in several countries. The easing reading did not last a day, and the earlier withdrawal of the outward-spread reading now looks premature.

withdrawn.held: The AI share sell-off was moving towards losses partly taken on by Taiwanese public money, through its state funds and central bank.
withdrawn.undone: On 1 November no state buying was reported, and the same thread was read as AI money landing on a few chip and computing makers, with Micron staff payouts and Chinese results led by AI computing. The public-money reading rested on one edition and is not carried as the thread's direction.

withdrawn.held: The Iran war thread had turned to which governments carry the fuel price and which take more of it as revenue, with US-Iran talks stuck.
withdrawn.undone: On 2 November no fuel-tax argument appeared, Brent fell 2% to $111, Trump said talks were going well and the thread was about whether a strike or talks follow the US vote. The who-pays reading rested on Turkey's single tax rise and is not carried as the direction; its expectation of a second government raising a fuel tax is still open.

withdrawn.held: The AI spending thread had turned to how narrowly the gains land, on a few chip and computing makers and their staff.
withdrawn.undone: Late on 2 November the thread was about the build depending on borrowing, with Oracle and Meta raising about $20 billion each and Anthropic losing more than its revenue, and on governments and voters setting terms for data centres; no payouts were reported. The concentration reading rested on one edition and is not carried as the direction; its expectations stay open.

withdrawn.held: Late on 2 November the Iran thread was tilting towards talks, with prices falling on leaders' words while incidents at sea continued.

caseAgainst: This Chronicle rests on the editions since 26 October, with none stamped 28 October, 9 November or 15 and 16 November, drawn from whichever publishers the collection reads and capped in how many headlines each may supply. Of today's three narratives only one continues an earlier one by its own link, and it is marked tentative and its own case against says most of the frontier steps were under way before the Shenzhen meeting; one resumes, after seventeen editions, a pair of narratives this Chronicle had stopped carrying, and two were built from the site's notebook, so today's continuity is again largely produced by the brief and the site. I turned the Europe security thread's direction after a single day, and may be over-reading one day's reports as I over-read the day before. The data centre thread is kept apart from the AI financing thread by the rule on unlinked narratives, not by a difference in the events, and it rests on one day's sell-off on a day CNBC reported Anthropic raising $93.5 billion. The kept protest-date expectation fits loosely, since Gen Z marches are called repeatedly, and the trade deals thread still rests on a bargaining frame I withdrew on 19 November.
line: On 20 November 2026, a day after the Shenzhen declaration, Estonia sets a date to close its Russian crossings and the Nasdaq falls 5.37% as AI chip orders are cut.
revision: Two threads were begun: states offering to site and underwrite data centres, and young protesters met by police and courts, the second reviving narratives of 31 October and 1 November that the Chronicle had not carried. The Europe security thread's direction was turned from allies seeking talks with Moscow to frontier states fortifying, and the talks reading was withdrawn; the threads on the Nvidia case, long-range strikes and Europe's living-cost protests fell silent, and the standing was rewritten.
